new_statements.quote: According to my data, Asu has three clear phonemic contrasting level tones. I use diacritics above the vowels to mark the tones: the acute /ɑ́/ depicts /H/; the grave /ɑ̀/ depicts /L/; the macron /ɑ̄/ depicts /M/. [...] (p.105) Most of the words collected in this study were recorded in isolation. Word-final vowels, which technically are phrase final vowels as well, have a predictable increased duration. This increase is present on morphemes regardless of their segmental structure and the phonetic realization of tone. [...] (p.108) Therefore, regardless of word length, the vowel of the final syllable has a predictably longer duration. In polysyllabic words, the final vowel has twice the duration as non-final vowels.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Asu is described as a three-level-tone language (H, M, L on every CV/CGV syllable, all nine combinations attested on CV.CV nouns); the thesis makes no claim about word stress or accent. The only prominence-like regularity it reports is phonetic lengthening of the (phrase-/word-)final vowel in isolation forms, which the author attributes to final position, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal distribution notes: [H] pitch mostly non-final, contours mostly final; [LH] only after /L/, [HL] never after /L/.
new_statements.domain_note: All data are wordlist items recorded in isolation (word = phrase); author explicitly notes no paradigms or connected text, so no phrase-level prosody is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Passetti 2022 describes Asu (aum, asun1235; also called Abewa/Ebe), Nupoid, spoken south-east of Kontagora, Mariga LGA, Niger State, from Constanze Weise's wordlist recordings; same variety as the Glottolog languoid. Not to be confused with Asu (Tanzania, Pare/Chasu, asut1235).

This increase is present on morphemes regardless of their segmental structure and the phonetic realization of tone. sources.note: Nothing on word stress/accent. Ch.5 (p.65): three phonemic level tones H, M, L; [HL],[LH] contours analysed as allotones. Sec. 6.3 (pp.105-108): final vowel of isolation forms predictably ~2x longer, attributed to (phrase-)final position. Only 'stress' token (p.111) concerns Hungarian/Icelandic pre-tap vowels.
